reviews.text: DarkSwitch is a fantasy-themed city builder that clearly draws inspiration from Frostpunk. Fans of the genre will immediately notice familiar elements, but the game introduces its own unique twist through its vertical city design and the dangerous fog mechanic. Instead of expanding outward like in most city builders, players construct a settlement around the trunk and branches of a colossal tree, gradually building upward by adding platforms, structures, and connections between different levels. This vertical layout creates new logistical challenges as the city grows. The game blends traditional city-building systems with survival mechanics. Players must gather and manage resources, construct production buildings, research technologies, and maintain the well-being of their citizens while expanding the settlement. A major threat comes from the mysterious fog surrounding the tree. The fog can drive citizens into madness and hide hostile creatures that threaten the city. To protect the settlement, players must illuminate the surroundings, build defensive structures, and sometimes send expeditions into the fog to search for resources, ancient technologies, and clues about its origins.

It’s a pretty interesting game, reminiscent of Frostpunk. As usual, it’s all about making tough decisions, and your most important resource is, of course, your people. As usual, everyone’s against you—everyone’s out to screw you over. But I’d like to see even more research and production branches, and more complex chains. Although it might not be obvious in the first hour, you have to keep playing to find out. So far, it’s pretty interesting.

[h1]I recommend it - I requested a refund.[/h1] This is a really tough game to pin down. I think my conflicted thoughts on DarkSwitch are evident enough in my reviewing it positively, but ultimately preferring to have my money and time back. There's a lot of good here, and I think if you're super into Frostpunk for the city & resource management aspects alone, you'll probably get a lot out of this game. I bought this because I absolutely love Frostpunk 1, and really hoped this would capture some of that same magic, but for me, it just doesn't. The resource management, strategic city building, and tech trees all seem well fleshed-out to me. I think if you're a number cruncher, there will be plenty here for you to chew on (although some more hotkeys certainly wouldn't go amiss). However, this game made me realise how much of my appreciation of Frostpunk is wrapped up in all the elements outside of the management sim; the story, the oppressive atmosphere, the designs of the art and sound, and the absolutely stellar soundtrack. DarkSwitch unfortunately just doesn't hold a candle to it in these regards. I probably should've been able to guess this given such a generic and non-descript title as "DarkSwitch", but the world and the setting are painfully shallow fantasy slop. It reads like teenager's attempt to capture Tolkien, with pointy-eared humanoid "Arelians" (who seriously, definitely aren't elves, guys) from "Nelaai" or "Elaran" bandying about ridiculous terms like "ethnarc", and using mystical "solar" (pronounced sol-AAR) to fight "guzzles"... I mean for godsake, an evil religious order called the [b][i]Illuminarchy[/i][/b] shows up in the first couple of days. The seriously amateur writing is not helped in the slightest by the character interactions all being voice acted in some of the worst ESL readings out there. The game looks nice enough, but you won't find that strong sense of atmospheric dread which hangs over you from day dot in Frostpunk, despite the story attempting to set up similar stakes. The music, similarly, is just fine, but lacks a powerful identity and ultimately ends up becoming annoying and sometimes overbearing. Ultimately, I think the strategic city builder and resource management side of this game has a really strong foundation, and if that's all you care about, you should give this game a go. I would love this to be a success story, so I'm comfortable giving DarkSwitch a recommendation. The surrounding artistic elements sadly do not sell me, and unfortunately that's what I would need to remain invested in the world and gameplay, so it's just not for me.

If you're a player, the choice is very simple. If aesthetics are your top priority and you have more than 20 hours to spare, this game is for you. But if you don't want to deal with bugs, the possibility of losing a settlement you've been building for over 20 hours, the lack of features that any modern game would have, this game is not for you. For those who have taken the plunge: the image may stop lagging if you disable vertical synchronization and limit the frame rate through your graphics card settings. It worked for me. Don't dismantle your constructions, but move them instead (the game doesn't explain this, but building a new structure is more expensive and harder than moving an existing one). Don't let the spiders form large groups, you won't be able to defeat them without losing too many rangers. Get to the tech level (walker units) as quickly as possible, they save on workers. Break your production into THREE conditional mini-settlements for gatherers (wood, metal, gas), put houses and kitchens there, place towers, move to a new spot once the resources are depleted. Make save points often, the game has many bugs that will ruin you. Early in the game, there's only one controllable way to reduce the population's fear (not losing game), the event with patrol, which you send rangers on. You need to do this constantly and make sure their path is safe, because the monsters can block the road and destroy your rangers approaching, and if the monsters don't let you build towers and buildings on this path - the problem is unsolvable, pray. When moving buildings, there can be issues with monsters not allowing you to build towers and structures - unsolvable in late game, pray. Usually, I don't write reviews. But I've spent about 15 hours on this beta test (I played it as everyone did at the release, but due to bugs capable of breaking the game, I'm calling it a beta) and I have several questions for the developer: 1. Why do settlers eat strictly at the kitchen? 2. Why duplicate resources? I know the duplicate version is cheaper, I just don't understand why. Literally the idea is that you can build from wood or wooden planks, the look, shape, and function will be the same in any case. 3. Suppose you need rangers to kill a monster, and the monster has a skill that disables the attack order on it (looks like a mix of a woman and a centipede). How do you attack it? 4. Suppose you have a pack of 3-5 spiders and you need to get rid of them from a spot using rangers? (For those who are unaware: even fully upgraded rangers can't take on 2 spiders. Due to the limit of 1 ranger unit attacking 1 monster at a time.) 5. How do you build in fog, if you can't see anything and builders don't want to build/or they dead? (I can't phrase the question more accurately, builders have a life of their own which is hard to understand here.) 6. Why are taverns called taverns if people don't eat or spend time there? Wouldn't calling them rations factories make more sense? And why do kitchens upgrade to taverns if people don't eat there? 7. Why are spiders described as non-aggressive creatures in the game if they're among the most aggressive in the game? 8. Why are there spots across the map where visually I can place a building but I can't in reality? And why are there spots where I can both visually and according to the game interface (the green dots light up) place a building but in reality I can't, as the building won't place? 9. Why does the game force the player to waste resources on actions that are pointless? For example, building SIX warships that just hang on the balance without purpose? 10. (For those unaware: in the game, one monster attack creates 3-5 notifications for each character it attacks.) When mid-game your base is attacked by 5-6 monsters at once and your headphones are blasted by the sound of notifications, do you turn off sound or enjoy the insane cacophony? 11. How do you protect settlers when they're on a cable car above the fog, and monsters bite them from below, and notifications again tear your headphones with an insane amount of sounds? 12. Why do settlers still ride on a cable car that leads nowhere and is in a dormant state? And then they get beaten by monsters, and then your headphones are torn apart by the wail of notifications. 13. If a monster in-game doesn't allow you to build a tower, and it/they are objectively stronger than a pack of rangers, who do you pray to? 14. Would you recommend a game to anyone where there are no difficulty settings, the average play session is 20-50 hours, and at any stage (most likely after 10-15 hours) you can lose? For example, by building many taverns and enjoying how the settlement starves while being full of food. Or by doomstack spiders wiping out rangers in dozens. (For those unaware: only rangers can clear the fog off the map, and without them the entire economy simply won't work.) Now, for the actual review: If we set aside the massive amount of bugs that will ruin your 20-hour gaming experience, the game at best is mediocre. And for rather mundane reasons – it's made to look beautiful, but it's uncomfortable to use. There are no quick buttons. No interface size settings. The fog covering the screen can't be removed even during construction, and it's hard to understand what's happening during construction in the fog (you can feed a couple of monsters with your builders for hours without being able to drive them away). The game's mechanics want you to develop a long, interconnected chain of resource gathering on the map to protect every meter of the path (if you don't do this, you can't create a protective network, as the beam concentrators will constantly be destroyed by monsters), but at the same time, it wants you to constantly change resource gathering spots and gather simultaneously from different points (without using the network mechanics). In other words, it sets you opposite tasks just for the heck of it. Tasks often mislead you or waste your resources for no reason. Mostly for the sake of successful gameplay, the best tactic is to ignore the tasks. The most wonderful part? TONS of notification sounds that someone has scratched your settler, with no way to adjust these notifications. In summary, all the features that any other game has and we've gotten used to are completely ignored here. The developers seem to have no idea what features exist in games like Against the Storm, All Will Fall, Frostpunk, etc. Of course, all games except All Will Fall have already gone through their "beta tests" with players' money and time, but these games didn't set such ambitious goals for their release as Darkswitch. Conclusion: It turns out to be an amusing irony. Darkswitch has huge ambitions and aspirations (just describing each element separately would take me several pages of A4 format, 9-point font), but crucial player functions (convenience and comfort, absence of duplicated functions, absence of bugs, clear and understandable game experience, choice of difficulty, choice of mode, the ability to not stare at the fog for dozens of hours, trying to see the terrain through construction points or by zooming in, etc.) are missing. To put it figuratively, the developers are creators, they care about the aesthetics, they care about the idea, but how you'll use it doesn't matter to them, or it matters insufficiently for them to prioritize working on this first. If I were given a choice between having vague, buggy monsters yelling notifications about attacks in your earphones, or simply the ability to customize notifications/interface, I would choose the interface.

This game despite it's issues, had a game play loop that was fun and interesting. However, about half way through chapter 3, everything just stopped working. Now mind you, all the production systems were working fine up until this point. - Workers only working for 30 min in a 12 hour shift. - A pack of about 10-12 workers keep standing in a single spot doing nothing. They just stand there until they die of starvation. They don't go home between shifts or anything. Every time one dies, another takes its place. This has effectively stopped my game because people are no longer working and they are basically just killing themselves. Other issues: - Keymaps reset every time you start up a new game - Voice acting is very bad. Possibly AI. - Artwork is all AI - Music is bad to the point I shut it off immediately after starting the game the first time. (Not a great 1st impression) - Graphical draw distance is extremely low. So even on the highest settings. you constantly see the draw circle and have pop-in around it. - There's a giant tree branch that comes through your main hub platform and is pointed dirtectly at the player. So you basically have a tree branch in your face all game. - The statistical screen showing production/usage is bad. Some of the categories are repeated multiple times while other catergories are flat out wrong. - Injured people will go to an unmanned medical facility and just sit there until you man it. (This needs to be setup like Frostpunk and be fobidden unless it has staff) - The game frequently gives you quest objectives that cannot be completed. - There is an advanced materials system but the game does not tell you how to make these advanced materials. This all being said, it was an interesting concept and despite it's flaws, I was enjoying the game. Right up until all my production broke. I posted these and other issues on the forums to give the devs a chance to respond or address, but the issues were not addressed or aknowledged.

I do not recommend the game in its current state, especially not at its current price of around €30. The game has a lot of potential. The atmosphere is strong, the visuals are beautiful, and I did have some genuinely enjoyable moments once I started to understand how everything works. However, the game currently feels too unfinished, unclear, and unstable to recommend. There are too many bugs and too many situations where you can lose a long settlement because of mechanics that are either poorly explained, badly balanced, or possibly broken. I had to restart three or four times just to understand the game properly, and I eventually lost a 54-day run because fear kept increasing endlessly, even though everything was covered by crystal lamps and defended. At that point, I could not do anything anymore. Many issues reported by other players match my own experience. Monsters can block important paths, spiders can gather into groups that are extremely hard to deal with, settlers sometimes take unsafe or confusing routes, and building defenses where you need them can become impossible. When this happens in the mid or late game, it can ruin many hours of progress. The game also lacks many basic quality-of-life features that would make the experience much better: UI scaling, clearer notifications, better camera controls, useful shortcuts, clearer building placement feedback, better pathing information, and more options to customize alerts. The UI is very small, the camera feels slow, and attack notifications can become overwhelming when several monsters attack at once. The fog and resource systems also feel contradictory. The game asks you to build long protected resource chains across the map, but at the same time resources get depleted and you constantly have to move gathering areas. This creates a lot of frustration, especially when fog hides what is happening and builders or rangers can die without the situation being clear. Some mechanics feel unfinished or badly explained. Airships mostly feel like simple point-and-click exploration and resource gathering. Some technologies seem useless, bugged, or too unclear to use properly. For example, I could not get the scout-tracking technology to work. Some quests also feel vague, misleading, or bugged, and events often trigger too abruptly. The heroes also need more work. Several abilities feel either too weak, unclear, bugged, or irrelevant once your base is properly lit and defended. The same goes for some buildings and systems, such as taverns, duplicated resources, patrols, rangers, and monster behavior, which all need clearer explanations and better balance. Overall, Darkswitch has great ideas and a very strong visual identity, but right now it feels more like an unfinished beta than a polished release. I think the developers have created an interesting world and concept, but the player experience needs much more attention: fewer bugs, better balance, clearer systems, difficulty settings, improved UI, better feedback, and more quality-of-life features. For now, I cannot recommend it at €30. With more updates, polish, and bug fixes, it could become a very good game, but in its current state it is too frustrating and unreliable.

This is a great game with a nice story and gameplay but that is bogged down by quite a few bugs and bad design choices. Lets start with the good stuff: - Great thematic world building - Most base mechanics are nice and intuitive. The advanced resources are a nice touch for base management decisions, use the inefficient raw materials or wait to refine them first? - Beautiful art direction - Nice story decisions - Decent balanced difficulty for the 1st half of the game (more on that later). Minor annoyances: - Voice acting is... weird to put it mildly - Cinematics have 20 year old graphics, which I actually found kind of endearing :D - The main characters act very erratic at times and are very unlikable as a result: [spoiler] Valfidis is someone who is doing his best to save his civilization, but keeps acting like a petty spoiled brat at times. Ginoa is a merciless and violent captain that would do anything to attain her goal... until she isnt... until she becomes an idealistic imbecile that would rather risk the extermination of her civilization in order to attempt to "save everyone", despite being told that it is impossible by Neammos. (She got lucky at the end, is all im gonna say) Neammos is the only likable hero that has even a semblance of intellect, but that intellect is called into doubt at the end when he surrenders to Ginoa when she bluffs that she will kill everyone if she does not get her way... [/spoiler] Now for the bad stuff: - The game has a lot of bugs, especially when it comes to enemies. Hopefully they will be fixed eventually - The overworld map camera is too slow and lack a decent zoom out view. When a mission tells you to scout a thing on X region, you have to VERY SLOWLY move over every region name until you find the one you need. - There is a terrible design decision on the start of chapter one where you have 2 scout points, the fishing place and the lumberjack place. If you choose the lumberjack place first, congratulations, you lost. Time to reload the checkpoint. For unknown reasons, building the fishing shack is locked behind that first scout area, so if you scout the lumberjack, by the time the scouts are ready for the next one you are out of food since you dont have the building to get it. Can you guess what is the cost for scouting the fishing place? Food... - I did not like the way watchtowers operate. Until you can add weapons on them, they are very slow to react to threats causing you to lose resources or even deaths - Solar and its advanced form crystalline. Normally you use planks (advanced resource of wood), which then gets replenished by refining your wood which in turn is replenished by your gatherers. Unlike the other resources you DO NOT refine solar into crystalline, you simply gather it (with advanced gathering buildings). That means that solar is a WORTHLESS resource. You use crystalline and then you gather more of it, while your solar remains unchanged... why does it even exist then? - Terrible pacing and difficulty scaling after the halfway mark of the campaign. There are finite resources and you have to relocate once they run out, or just split up your gatherers so that they do not deplete everything fast. You should also invest as early as you can on advances resources since they effectively double the available resources. I only had to relocate each resource type twice. Until you gain access to outposts... after some point (around day 40ish, not sure), I was done with resources. My metal and gas areas were depleted but I didnt even bother to rellocate, I had infinite resources (1000+ of each resource, raw and advanced until the end of the game). Coupled with 2 max level healing buildings I was done with the game... literally. I put it on fast forward and watched a movie while returning to check on events and story choices. The latter quarter of the game was me being bored out of my mind doing nothing. The overworld map was filled to the brim with cargo locations which I never needed (probably didnt even scout more than 20 cargo locations). Endless waiting until the ending event, and even that was anticlimactic with all my watchtowers and light orb thingies. Why am I recommending this? 20 out of my 23hours were quite a bit of fun. I even restarted a couple of times because I messed up with either food or sickness, but that is part of the fun for me. If you want a semi difficult base survival game to scratch that frostpunk itch, this is it. If you want an easy game you can play for the story you might wanna stay clear since there is no difficulty option (so far)

Overall, I'm a fan of the game. I loved Frostpunk and this was clearly heavily influenced by it with some twists making the game its own. The story was fairly interesting, the mechanics overall were solid and I would absolutely recommend it. With that said, be prepared for some frustration even if you really like the concept and the game as a whole. I'm not going to list all the issues I ran into but here are a couple that really stood out: - Be prepared for some performance issues later in the game - The pacing of the story feels wildly wrong or off, especially if you focus on doing all the research / exploring as quick as you can. Towards the later half I just sat there sitting on max speed alt - tabbed waiting for something to happen - A lot of the combat or exploration feels very hollow - things just "happen" and are instantly resolved with no real oompf to them - Enemies do not have HP bars - without spoiling I will say this can get very frustrating - I did not feel as if my choices really mattered all that much outside of their instant effects. I would have even liked to see a stats screen at the end seeing how other people chose certain events etc. - It's unclear how to resolve certain things or maybe I just missed the best way of going about it. For example, your people can get tired. How do you resolve that? Probably by adding in third shifts, but have fun running around clicking on all your buildings trying to find which ones you may not have third shifts on yet. - The UI just has some general frustrations similar to the above point, things are tough to find, don't cycle properly, you'll often get interrupted by auto save or other events and have to re-click on things etc. Again, I would still recommend the game, and I had a good time, it just might be worth waiting for a couple of fixes or additions to the game first.

Strong concept, execution could use some work. Building vertically to escape madness-inducing fog is a neat concept, and having to devote resources to keeping the fog back simply to keep your economy going adds a (to my knowledge) unique twist to builder/survival games. The blend of fantasy and solar/steampunk elements scratches an itch I've been trying to get from my game library for a while and I'm looking forward to seeing all the game has to offer. That being said, I hope the devs continue to work on the game as there are a number of things that could use it. Moving the camera around the map is a little slow, which makes controlling your ranger squads or adjusting building staff a little cumbersome. It also seems as though the rangers specifically, which act as a sort of military/scouting force, lose a lot of their usefulness after Act 1 or so and end up serving as little more than guards assigned to your various defensive towers. Second, while this could just be my luck, the story mode has bursts of pop-up notifications for quests and story elements that hit in such quick succession that there's barely time to breathe before gameplay grinds to a halt so the oddly-voiced characters can have a conversation. It's a jarring game element that pulls you completely out of whatever menu you were in to the point that I've forgotten what I was doing several times. It's also worth noting that the dialogue does not match up to the captions during these cutscenes, and the line delivery is often very strange; I'm tempted to say that the cast is largely voiced by AI. Ultimately, I'm recommending Dark Switch because it shows a lot of promise from what seems to be a new developer and I want to see them push the game to reach its full potential.

This is an excellent colony builder in the vein of Frostpunk and Cliff Empires and Ixion (and the incoming pirate one, Corsair Cove). I don't find value in comparing these titles other than to say that they scratch a similar itch. DarkSwitch is steampunk elves in a world increasingly twisted by a creeping fog, akin to Stephen Kings 'The Mist' (called The Shroud). Large world trees (Aredetis Trees I think they are called) are your hope as you build structures around them and above the fog. Resources like wood, food, and metal can only be found on the ground, forcing you to also build on the land and contend with the Shroud. So far I am 14 hours in and having a great time. What is here is worth the price tag hands down, and the mini events offer replay value. The game feels good in all regards, it runs well, pacing is good with challenges and progress, complexity of tech and new buildings is diverse without being cumbersome, There are some smaller quality of life things I would like to see, and Devs responded favorably to comments in forums (more patches and changes based on feedback and development decisions incoming), with the last patch as of posting being 1.1.2 on June 24. The Voice Acting (English localization) is interesting. Eastern European Elves? (Triple E!). Initially I didn't like it, but after 14 hours so far, i found myself happy to have the Voice Acting than not for the encounters (its just some NPC dialogue is voiced, not every encounter). I HIGHLY recommend giving the demo a try if you can. Moreover, while most games are 'worth it' with a big enough discount, few games, imo, are worth it even if there is not a discount currently, and I count DarkSwitch as among them.

Overall, I highly recommend Dark Switch to anyone looking for a fresh take on the genre with a great story.
